I'm an avid runner who runs around 4-5 hours a week (5Ks and 10Ks). This summer I completed my first half-marathon.

As I kept walking past the finish line, I appreciated how alive the muscles in my body felt and the gentle burn of the sun on my sweaty skin. It was exhilarating.

I was in a closed-off post-race segment full of volunteers. One of them draped a medal around my neck, the next one gave me a goodie bag, etc, etc. Awesome times, awesome feelings. The last segment was full of huge boxes with size markers on them. You might see where this is going.

I walk up to the S boxes, and the volunteers smile apologetically, saying they're all out. No problem - this is my first half marathon, I got beaten by a lot of people. Still...a shirt to remember the day would have been nice. I headed back to XS, but found they were out as well. I walked forward to M...also empty.

Mind you, I wasn't dead last. There were still LOADS of people crossing the finish line just behind me. I'd venture to say at least a quarter of the runners had yet to finish the race. I debated getting an L...but it wouldn't even be comfortable to sleep in.

I kept walking to get out of the post-race segment, and found they were almost out of the Ls too. Oh well. Poor planning by the organisers, right? Oh wait, what's this? keep walking Are those XL boxes? But...those are almost full up...there's got to be 2000 shirts in those! keep walking And...XXL?!? The volunteers look bored. Those boxes are still sealed! This is a half-marathon. The amount of people who could fit an XXL probably number in the single digits...Then my jaw dropped. As I kept walking I saw that there was a final stack of boxes labelled XXXL.

I'd estimate overall there were probably about 5-6000 unclaimed shirts at the end of the day because the race organisers thought it made sense to divide the amount of shirts EVENLY across all sizes, even though anything above an L makes NO SENSE at an athletic event.

But I want to hear from you people with experience with either or both technologies. Which one do you prefer and why? For me, I can't say much since I'm just a student with budget cuts who can't afford a cutting edge $400 monitor with a GTX 980Ti or a Radeon Fury X :P

Just like any other battle of technology, there will be pros and cons for both.

Humbly I think it's still too early for anyone to even make a proper list for either one, though.

Having two competing techs is a shame. Of course non propitiatory (Freesync) would be ideal. But when one finally 'wins' the marketplace will be a better place. I really hate the idea of being locked into one brand if I buy said monitor.....

Totally agree. Another overpriced piece of technology. And its impact is not that big.

Since when does something new make your old stuff obsolete? You yourself decide when something stops being good enough for you.

FreeSync is a royalty free technology, that can be implemented into a monitors controller to remove tearing and stuttering to the degree of the manufacturers will. I can't see a bad thing about it. There are even monitors, that have received the FreeSync upgrade afterwards through firmware.

I have to disagree. I have a freesync setup and it works well. The biggest difference is when running 60fps and below (easy to do with a single card and max details at 1440p), motion is noticeably smoother and more consistent.

Also it doesn't require a "bunch of crap" to work, the controller and firmware in the screen just has to support it. As it's now an adopted extension to vesa there's nothing stopping more monitor manufacturers from adding it. Unlike G-Sync there is no special hardware in the monitor itself.

Eliminates tearing without VSync stutter, a luxury item? I beg to differ. It doesn't require "a bunch of crap". I don't even know what you're talking about there. Plug your monitor in, activate the feature in your graphics control panel and voilà, it works.

As for the differences between the two, I heard there are some, mostly related to the lowest frequency at which the system can work. Both bring a serious visual improvement regardless, so I'd guess FSync will become dominant.

I picked up two R9 290Xs. I also picked up the Freesync Acer 27inch 144hz monitor. All that cost me less than 1k. You'll spend more than that for a single 980ti and the equivalent G-sync Nvidia monitor.

I like having a good setup, but I'm also cost aware. I feel like I have a pretty good cost-performance setup for nabbing 144 fps in most titles.

I'd say get what ever video card you can afford then get a monitor that your gpu will work with. If you can't afford a G-Sync / Freesync right now then don't worry about it. The only one I've used is G-Sync and it's great for games that fluctuate frame rates. Climbing a major mountain is no small task, whether it's Everest, Kilamanjaro, McKinley (which is technically a longer climb, as its base is lower than that of Everest), or any other. It's not a matter of fitness and toughness. It's a matter of luck and survival.

Only about 1 out of 4 people who try to climb Everest manage to reach the top. Among first-time the rate is 1 of 3, because they don't know enough to avoid the risks that could kill them. The top of Everest is past a barrier where your body stops taking oxygen in; the air is so thin that every time you breathe, the air takes oxygen out of your body. On top of that, you need excellent weather once you are at the highest base camp, or you will be trapped. And, even if you start with perfect weather, you have to reach the top by about 2 PM, or the weather will close in and kill you on your way down.

There are far fewer people there than on a mountain like McKinley (due to the fees and general inaccessibility), so if you have problems no one will find and save you.

Everest is as much a survivalist expedition as it is a mountain climbing expedition.

To misquote "The Bard of Avon" "To Reload or not to Reload that is the Question?""

Well here is the economics of Reloading.

If you only have one or two weapons that you take out once or twice a year for hunting, then it really doesn't make sense to invest in reloading equipment.

If you are a gun collector that only collect guns but maybe shoots them three or four times a year and then only 20 to 40 rounds per trip it doesn't really make sense to invest in the equipment to reload.

Now if you have an AR-15 and you shoot twice a month and shoot up 5 mags at a time then you probably should be reloading. Or if you shoot some odd caliber then reloading is the way to go.

One last thing that should be considered is powder, because that is going to be the major expense and the bottle neck. If you have a large number of firearms that you shoot a lot in lot of different calibers then you should select a smokeless powder that works OK in all of them and buy a lot of that powder. The price per pound of powder that comes in a 8 lb caddie is a lot less per pound than (8) one pound canisters. However if you are one of those guys that wants to wring every ounce of performance out of your fire arm then buy 1 lb canisters of the powder that your fire arm likes the best. Of course that being said, if you are a prepper and all you want is your smoke stick to go bang when you pull the trigger, then by all means buy the cheapest stuff around and load up 10.000 rounds of the stuff.

One last thing to remember is to work up your load. I have seen two expensive bolt action rifles from the same manufacturer and the same model with the same amount of usage, shot side by side on the same day with the same ammo. Rifle #1 will put all the bullets in the black and the groups can be covered by a tuna fish can. Rifle #2 will dammed near put all the bullets in the same hole. Go Figure.
